questions.skill: What resampling simulates
questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: Why can resampling a random sample (drawing with replacement) show how sample means vary?
questions.prompt_markup: Why can resampling a random sample (drawing with replacement) show how sample means vary?

choices.text: Resampling collects new data from the whole population each time it is done.
Resampling always gives the true population mean as the center.
Resampling removes all chance variation from the sample means.
The resamples act like new samples from a population that looks like the sample.

questions.correct_answer: The resamples act like new samples from a population that looks like the sample.
questions.grading_note: The sample stands in for the population. The others are false: resampling uses only the original sample, does not give the true mean, and does not remove chance variation.

questions.prompt: How is the margin of error for one mean related to judging a difference between two means?
questions.prompt_markup: How is the margin of error for one mean related to judging a difference between two means?

choices.text: A difference between two means never varies by chance, so it does not need any measure of chance variation.
The margin of error for one mean is always equal to the difference between the two group means.
Both ask how much a statistic varies by chance; a difference is meaningful only if it is large compared with that variability.
They are unrelated: one uses the data, and the other uses only the number of subjects in each group.

questions.correct_answer: Both ask how much a statistic varies by chance; a difference is meaningful only if it is large compared with that variability.
questions.grading_note: Both compare a statistic with its chance variability.
